children.text: The Calaguas island group off the coast of Camarines Norte is famous for Mahabang Buhangin, a beach as fine as flour. With little electricity or amenities, camping under a tent while listening to the waves and watching the Milky Way gives travelers who love camping and off-the-grid beaches an unforgettable experience.
The Calaguas group is a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean (Philippine Sea), about
30km
off the coast of Camarines Norte in southeastern Luzon and about
200km

in a straight line from Manila. It consists of three large islands (Tinaga, Guintinua, and Maculabo) plus small islands and rock islets; Maculabo falls under Paracale, and the rest under Vinzons. Travelers almost always head to Mahabang Buhangin (meaning "long sand"), a beach on Tinaga Island, which is about
8km
long. True to its name, the long stretch of white sand is as fine as flour, and gently sloping grassy hills rise behind the beach, giving it the feel of a grassland meadow.

This island was long called "Boracay's old self" because it has barely been developed. With no power grid, nights rely entirely on generators and solar lighting, and lodging centers on beach tents and simple huts. As visitor numbers have grown recently, hut-style resorts, paid showers, paid charging services, and even satellite internet in some areas have appeared, but there are still no big hotels or shopping streets.

On clear nights there is almost no light pollution, so you can see the Milky Way and a sky full of stars, and in the morning you can climb the hill behind the beach to watch the sun rise from the sea. Getting there takes several changes of bus, tricycle, and bangka and isn't easy, but for anyone who can enjoy the journey itself as part of the trip, this ranks among Luzon's finest beaches.

It suits young travelers who enjoy camping, groups of friends, and travelers who want to spend a whole day doing nothing on a quiet beach. It doesn't suit travelers who need air conditioning and hot showers.
Plan for at least
2 days, 1 night
, or
3 days, 2 nights
for a relaxed pace. The boat ride alone takes
2–3 hours
one way, and getting from Manila to the beach takes
12–15 hours
one way, so a day trip isn't realistic. Costs fall into two broad patterns. A join tour from Manila that bundles bus, boat, tent, and meals costs about
per person, a join tour that you meet up with in Vinzons costs about
, and a DIY trip that a group arranges on its own costs about
per person (based on April–May 2026 guides; check the operator's latest rates).
Sand soft enough to sink your feet into stretches the length of the beach. The shallower water at low tide is good for swimming, and the water shines brightest in the afternoon.
Climb the grassy hill behind the beach for about
15–30 minutes
and the beach and surrounding islands come into view all at once. Leave around
, before sunrise, to catch the sun rising over the sea.
Pitching a tent and falling asleep to the sound of the waves is the core experience of Calaguas. On moonless nights, the Milky Way appears sharp and clear.
Charter a bangka to explore nearby deserted-island beaches, snorkeling spots, and rocky cliff coastlines. It's best to head out in the morning on calm-wave days.
Fish, squid, and pork bought at the Vinzons market are grilled by the boatman or hut owner. Eating barbecue on the beach at sunset is the highlight of a Calaguas trip.
You can rent a kayak or snorkel in the shallow water in front of the beach. The coral patches aren't large, but the clear water makes it easy to spot small tropical fish.

children.text: Taking a surf lesson or watching the sunset at Bagasbas Beach in Daet on the way back makes the trip even richer.
Balagbag, a small island next to Tinaga, is reached by bangka; climb the hill for a little over
10 minutes
and the dark red rocky shore, emerald water, and the long white beach of Tinaga across the way all fit into one view. The entrance fee is reported to be about
, making it a good first stop for island hopping. Fees may change, so confirm on site.

Buses to Daet such as DLTB and Superlines run daily from the terminals around Cubao, Pasay, and Buendia in Manila, taking about
7–10 hours
and costing about
. If you take a night bus you arrive at dawn and can catch the morning boat the same day. From Daet to Vinzons takes about
30 minutes–1 hour
by jeepney or van (about
), and from Vinzons town to the port about
10–15 minutes
by tricycle.
The closest commercial airport is Naga Airport (WNP). Since
March 29, 2026
, propeller aircraft have been banned from Manila's Ninoy Aquino Airport, so there are no direct Manila–Naga flights, and now it takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Clark on a Cebgo flight. From downtown Naga to Daet takes about
2–3 hours

by bus or van, so even if you fly, the total travel time is not greatly reduced. To save time, taking the first morning flight and catching an afternoon boat the same day, or spending a night in Daet, is realistic.

There are two ports for Calaguas. Tours and resort packages mostly use Minaogan Port in Vinzons (Pajares Port, the tourist hub), and boats also leave from the Paracale fishing port. A chartered bangka is the norm: a small boat for 4–6 people costs about
round trip, and a large boat for 15–20 people about
. The crossing takes about
2–3 hours
one way from Vinzons and about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes

from Paracale. On peak-season weekends there are also shared bangkas that sell seats individually once enough people are gathered. Using a travel agency's join tour (round-trip bus from Manila, boat, and tent included) makes preparation far easier.
Superlines runs a direct night bus from Cubao, Manila to Paracale, taking about
10 hours
, with air-conditioned bus fares of about
. From Daet, a van to Paracale takes about
1–2 hours
and costs about
, and from Paracale town to the fishing port it is a short tricycle ride. Philtranco's air-conditioned Pasay–Daet bus costs about
. Schedules and fares change, so check before you leave.
From Manila to Daet is about
342km
, which takes about
7–10 hours
by bus. The usual approach is to leave the car near Vinzons port or the Paracale fishing port, and parking is reported to cost around
(it varies by operator). When leaving your car, check in advance whether it can stay for two days or longer and who is responsible for it while it is stored.
Tinaga Island has almost no paved roads, so you get around on foot between the beach, the hills, and the village. Island hopping nearby costs about
per bangka, and if you choose a local guide for the viewpoint hill it costs about
per person.
Calaguas is exposed to the Pacific, so sea conditions vary greatly by season. The best time is from
March
to
June

, when winds are light and the sea is calm, making boat travel comfortable and the water at its clearest. During weekends and Holy Week in this period, local campers crowd in heavily, so a weekday visit is recommended.
From
November
to
February
, the northeast monsoon Amihan causes high waves that frequently suspend bangka service, and the coast guard often bans departures. From
July
to
October
is the rainy and typhoon season, with frequent typhoons passing through Bicol, making it hard to plan a trip.
The beach has almost no shade, so the midday heat index is very high. Sun exposure is especially strong in
April–May
, so bringing a tarp or shade canopy makes staying much more comfortable.
Many guides name
February–May
as the most reliable period. The water is clearest in
February–April
and it is busiest in
March–May
June
is when the southwest monsoon (Habagat) begins, so sea conditions differ from year to year, and tour operators stop sailing if the waves are rough. The typhoon risk is highest in
September–November
, and in
December–January
northeast monsoon swells are large, so it comes down to luck. Bicol is typhoon-prone: when Super Typhoon Carding struck in
September 2022
, about 100 tourists were stranded on the island but all were safe, and during Tropical Storm Trami in late
, Daet saw record-breaking rainfall.

On-island lodging falls into three broad types. The first is beach camping — bring your own tent and pay only a site fee, or rent a tent on the spot. The second is nipa huts and small resorts behind the beach, with rooms equipped with a fan or a simple mattress at about

per night. The third is a group camp included in a travel agency package, with meals, tents, and the boat all bundled together, which is convenient for first-timers. On the night before or after, it's best to stay at a hotel in downtown Daet (about
per night).

The island has small shops and huts selling meals, but choices are limited and prices are higher than on the mainland. So most people buy fish, squid, pork, rice, fruit, water, and ice at the Vinzons market before heading in. Give the boatman or hut owner a tip and they'll cook the rice and grill the meat for you. Camarines Norte is known for its small, sweet Formosa pineapples, well worth trying. In Daet, you can eat Bicolano dishes like Bicol Express and laing cheaply.

Resorts on the island that are often mentioned include Calaguas White Sand Resort, Waling-Waling Resort, Calaguas Paradise Resort, and I Love Calaguas. According to an April 2026 guide, an open-style hut at I Love Calaguas costs about
per night (5 people) and an enclosed one about
, while an air-conditioned hut at Waling-Waling is about
. Pitching your own tent costs a site fee of about
, and renting a dome tent costs about
per night. Showers have no hot water and cost about
per bucket or about
for unlimited use, and the toilet costs about
per use. Huts fill up early in peak season, so book ahead.
There are no ATMs on the island, and cards are almost never used. Withdraw all the cash you'll need in Daet and bring plenty of small bills.
With no power grid, charging depends on paid generators or solar chargers. It's a good idea to bring two or more high-capacity power banks.
Phone signal only reaches weakly at some spots on the beach. It's a good idea to let family know your itinerary in advance.
Plan on at least 3 liters of water per person per day; ice and a cooler make food storage much easier.
The beach has little shade, so bring a tarp, hat, rash guard, and reef-safe sunscreen.
Pitch your tent well above the high-tide line, and use sand stakes or sandbags to guard against wind.
It's best to agree clearly before departure on whether the bangka fare is round trip, whether island hopping is included, and what time you'll return.
Sunrise photos are best taken on top of Tinaga hill, and Milky Way photos at the end of the beach away from any lights.
Electricity from the island's generators usually comes on only from
6 PM to 6 AM
. Some huts sell Starlink satellite Wi-Fi for about
per
1 hour 30 minutes
, but the speed is on the slow side.
Viewpoint hills and each island charge a separate environmental fee or entrance fee. The low hill costs about
, the high hill about
, and Balagbag Island about
, so bring plenty of small bills in
, and
denominations.
If high waves lead the coast guard to ban departures, you could be stranded on the island, so it's best to leave at least a day of buffer before your flight or any important schedule.
Always wear a life vest on the bangka, and never board an overloaded boat.
Waste disposal facilities are limited, so take back all the trash you bring in. It's best to avoid glass bottles on the beach.
There's almost no lighting at night, so you need a flashlight when moving around the beach, and you must never swim in the sea at night after drinking.
Mosquitoes and sand flies are common, so bring insect repellent.
Environmental fee and island-entry rules are changed frequently by the Vinzons tourism authority, so check the latest notices before you go.

There is no official lifeguard on the island and the nearest mainland hospital can only be reached by boat, so evacuation in an emergency is difficult. In the marine protected area, fishing and collecting coral or shells are prohibited, and snorkeling must follow the posted guidance.
